events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: The first of three Reconstruction-era amendments was ratified eight months after a brutal civil war ended, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States except as punishment for crime. The exception clause would become the legal scaffolding for convict-leasing systems that reproduced plantation labor for another 80 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1865 — when Georgia became the 27th state to ratify. Mississippi officially ratified only in 1995, and didn't certify it until 2013, due to a paperwork oversight.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Freedom Summer Murders
events.blurb: Three voter-registration volunteers — two Jewish New Yorkers and a local Black civil rights worker — disappeared after being arrested for an alleged traffic violation, released at night, and abducted by Klansmen near a Mississippi town. Their bodies were found 44 days later, bulldozed into an earthen dam. A massive FBI manhunt — the first major civil rights intervention by the Bureau — cracked the case.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1964 — Philadelphia, Mississippi. James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner. The state refused to prosecute; federal civil-rights conspiracy charges netted seven convictions. The ringleader, Edgar Ray Killen, was finally convicted of manslaughter in 2005 at age 80.

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Treaty of Paris Recognizes American Independence
events.blurb: Representatives of Britain and the United States signed a peace treaty at a Paris hotel ending the American Revolutionary War. Britain recognized the new country's independence; set its western boundary at the Mississippi River; and granted generous fishing rights off Newfoundland. Spain and France signed separate treaties the same day ending their parallel wars. Britain had lost the largest and richest colony in the world.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1783 — Hotel d'York, Paris. American negotiators: Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, John Jay. The United States shrewdly kept its French ally out of the negotiations, violating the Franco-American alliance's terms, and secured better borders as a result.

events.title: Reign of Terror Begins
events.blurb: The French revolutionary government, governed for nearly a year by a Committee of Public Safety dominated by a 35-year-old lawyer, formalized terror as an instrument of state by enacting a law declaring "terror the order of the day." Over the following ten months, revolutionary tribunals sentenced roughly 17,000 people — noblewomen, priests, rival republicans, peasants, whoever — to the guillotine. The terror ended only when the committee turned on its own leader.
events.revealBlurb: September 5, 1793 — the phrase. Maximilien Robespierre would himself be guillotined on July 28, 1794 (9 Thermidor), bringing the terror to an abrupt end. Total executions and prison deaths during the Terror: perhaps 40,000 across the country.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.blurb: The United Nations General Assembly, meeting in a Paris exhibition hall, adopted a declaration of 30 articles enumerating rights that every human being was to be considered entitled to by virtue of humanity itself. The document's drafting committee, chaired by the widow of a U.S. president, had spent two years negotiating across ideological and cultural lines. No state voted against; eight abstained.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1948 — Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. Adopted 48-0 with 8 abstentions (Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia, South Africa). Translated into over 500 languages — more than any other document. December 10 is now International Human Rights Day.

events.title: First Woman Prime Minister
events.blurb: The widow of an assassinated South Asian island-nation prime minister was sworn in as his successor, becoming the first woman to lead a national government anywhere in the world. She had entered politics only after her husband's murder the previous year. She would serve three separate terms over four decades, dying in office at age 84.
events.revealBlurb: July 21, 1960 — Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). She led a non-aligned left-of-center government; her daughter Chandrika became president 34 years later. She died on November 13, 2000, after casting her vote in a general election.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Benazir Bhutto Becomes PM
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Oxford and Harvard educated politician whose father had been hanged by a previous military government was sworn in as prime minister of a large South Asian Muslim-majority country, becoming the first woman to head the government of any Muslim-majority state. Her ruling coalition was fragile; she would be dismissed twice on corruption charges and would be assassinated 19 years later while campaigning for a third term.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1988 — Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan. She was assassinated in Rawalpindi on December 27, 2007, after a campaign rally. Her 19-year-old son Bilawal was named co-chair of her party within days.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: Kitchen Debate
events.blurb: At the opening of an American National Exhibition in Moscow, a U.S. vice president and a Soviet premier stood beside a model suburban kitchen and argued about consumer goods, nuclear weapons, and the relative virtues of their systems. Live cameras caught every jabbing finger. Polaroid prints of the exchange appeared in American newspapers within days.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1959 — Richard Nixon and Nikita Khrushchev at Sokolniki Park. The kitchen was a General Electric display. Nixon's ability to hold his own in the unscripted shouting match boosted his 1960 presidential prospects (though not quite enough).

events.title: INF Treaty Signed
events.blurb: At a White House ceremony, the American and Soviet leaders signed a treaty requiring both sides to destroy every intermediate-range nuclear missile they possessed — the first arms-control agreement that actually cut existing weapons rather than capping their growth. Within three years, 2,692 missiles had been verifiably dismantled.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1987 — Reagan and Gorbachev. Both Pershing IIs and SS-20s were eliminated. The treaty was abandoned in 2019 after mutual accusations of cheating, ending a 32-year cornerstone of European security.

events.title: German Reunification
events.blurb: On a crisp autumn evening, a huge black, red, and gold flag was raised in front of the Reichstag building as the East German state ceased to exist and its 16 million citizens became part of the unified federal republic. Forty-five years of partition, imposed by four occupying armies, ended at the stroke of midnight. Crowds sang the national anthem for the first time as one country.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1990 — the date is now German Unity Day. The integration cost West Germany over €2 trillion over three decades. Many eastern cities still empty out; many western taxpayers still grumble about the "solidarity surcharge."

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Sgt. Pepper's Released
events.blurb: A four-person British pop group released an album that redefined popular music's ambitions. Recorded over 129 days, it experimented with orchestral arrangements, studio sound effects, Indian classical instruments, a pig from a farmyard, and a final 42-second tape loop designed to be audible to dogs. The cover showed the band as an imaginary marching band in front of a crowd of cardboard-cutout cultural heroes. It sat at number one on both sides of the Atlantic for months.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1967 (UK) — Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band by the Beatles. Peter Blake designed the cover; the cardboard figures included Marilyn Monroe, Karl Marx, and Edgar Allan Poe. Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr are the only surviving Beatles today.

events.title: Altamont Free Concert
events.blurb: A free Rolling Stones concert at a dusty California motor speedway, hastily organized as a West Coast Woodstock, instead became the counterculture's dark counterpart. Hells Angels motorcycle gang members had been hired to provide stage security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. Fights broke out throughout the day; during the Rolling Stones' set an Angel stabbed an 18-year-old audience member to death within a metre of the stage.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1969 — Altamont Speedway, California. The victim was Meredith Hunter, 18; the Angel who stabbed him, Alan Passaro, was acquitted on grounds of self-defense. The 1970 documentary "Gimme Shelter" captures the killing.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbit
events.blurb: A 58-centimeter aluminum sphere carrying four radio antennas was boosted into an elliptical low Earth orbit, becoming the first artificial satellite. Its rhythmic beeping was receivable by amateur radio operators worldwide for 21 days.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First American in Space
events.blurb: Alan Shepard rode a Redstone rocket on a 15-minute suborbital arc reaching 187 km altitude, becoming the first American in space — 23 days after Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight. Unlike Gagarin's automated mission, Shepard manually controlled his capsule's attitude during the flight using a hand controller, though the arc itself was ballistic and unpowered.
events.revealBlurb: May 5, 1961 — Freedom 7. Shepard had been suited up and waiting in the capsule for four hours through repeated launch delays. At one point he radioed mission control: "Why don't you fix your little problem and light this candle?" His answer came 15 minutes later. He was weightless for only 5 minutes of the flight.

events.title: First Soft Moon Landing
events.blurb: The Soviet Luna 9 spacecraft landed intact on the Ocean of Storms, becoming the first vehicle to achieve a controlled soft landing on another world and transmit photographs from the surface. Its four petal-shaped panels opened to right the lander and deploy an antenna, then it sent back a panoramic image sequence over three sessions totaling nine images.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1966 — Luna 9. British radio astronomers at Jodrell Bank intercepted the transmission and noticed it used the same format as a standard wire-photo machine. They borrowed a Müller facsimile unit from a news agency and published the images before the Soviets released them officially — to Moscow's considerable irritation.

events.title: Galileo Enters Jupiter Orbit
events.blurb: NASA's Galileo spacecraft became the first to orbit an outer planet when it fired its main engine for 49 minutes to slow into Jupiter orbit. Simultaneously, a 339 kg atmospheric probe it had released five months earlier plunged into Jupiter's clouds and transmitted data for 58 minutes, surviving temperatures of 16,000 °C before being crushed by atmospheric pressure.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1995 — Galileo. The spacecraft's high-gain antenna failed to deploy fully in 1991, so the entire mission's data was re-routed through a low-gain antenna; engineers compressed the transmission protocols so thoroughly that Galileo sent back almost as much science as originally planned. During its eight years at Jupiter, it discovered evidence of a liquid water ocean beneath Europa's ice.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Confederate Attack on Fort Sumter
events.blurb: At 4:30 in the morning, Confederate artillery opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning a 34-hour bombardment that forced the Union to surrender and formally launched the deadliest war in American history. No one was killed in the bombardment itself — two Union soldiers died in a cannon accident during the surrender ceremony.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1861 — Charleston, South Carolina. The Confederacy fired over 4,000 shells at the fort; Union defenders fired roughly 1,000 back. Nobody died in combat during the entire engagement. Within four days, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, and four more states seceded to join the Confederacy.

events.title: Teapot Dome: Senate Investigation Opens
events.blurb: The Senate launched its first formal investigation into the Teapot Dome oil fields that autumn, following revelations that Interior Secretary Albert Fall had secretly leased federal naval petroleum reserves in Wyoming and California to private oil companies in exchange for personal cash loans and gifts totaling roughly $400,000. Fall would become the first U.S. Cabinet member ever convicted of a crime committed while in office.
events.revealBlurb: October 1923 — Washington, D.C. The oil companies that paid the bribes — Sinclair Oil and Pan American Petroleum — were acquitted at trial; only the man who took the bribes was convicted. President Harding died of a heart attack in August 1923, before the scandal fully broke.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: FDR's "Day of Infamy" Speech
events.blurb: A president delivered a 6-minute address to a joint session of his nation's legislature the morning after a surprise naval attack, opening with a phrase he had changed at the last moment from "world history" to something more damning, and closing with a request for a formal declaration of war that passed within hours with a single dissenting vote.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1941 — 81% of American adults listening by radio, the largest audience in broadcast history to that point. Congress voted 82-to-0 in the Senate, 388-to-1 in the House. The lone "no" vote, pacifist Jeannette Rankin of Montana, had also voted against entering World War I.

events.title: Fall of Tobruk
events.blurb: A fortified port city that had withstood a nine-month siege the previous year fell to an armoured assault in a single day, yielding 33,000 prisoners — including an entire South African division — along with 2,000 vehicles, 5,000 tons of food, and enough fuel to sustain the attacking force's advance for weeks.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1942. Churchill learned of Tobruk's fall while meeting Roosevelt in Washington — handed a pink slip of paper mid-meeting. Roosevelt's immediate response: "What can we do to help?" He arranged 300 Sherman tanks and 100 self-propelled guns for immediate shipment. The news triggered a no-confidence vote against Churchill in the House of Commons.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: Victory in Europe Day
events.blurb: Unconditional surrender documents were signed at an Allied headquarters on two successive nights in two different cities, and the moment the ceasefire took effect at one minute past eleven, millions of people in cities across a battered continent poured into the streets to celebrate the end of a conflict that had killed an estimated 70 to 85 million human beings.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1945. Germany signed the first surrender at Reims on May 7; a second signing in Berlin satisfied Soviet demands. Stalin proclaimed May 9 as Victory Day — still observed in Russia today. More than a million people celebrated in the streets across the UK. Churchill told the crowds from a Whitehall balcony: "God bless you all. This is your victory."

events.title: The Mother of All Demos
events.blurb: A 43-year-old Stanford Research Institute engineer delivered a 90-minute live demonstration to 1,000 conference attendees in San Francisco that showcased a computing system combining the mouse, windowing interface, hypertext links, real-time text editing, screen sharing, and video conferencing — all two decades before any of these became available on a commercial computer. The audience sat in stunned silence.
events.revealBlurb: December 9, 1968 — Douglas Engelbart at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. His live video link from his Menlo Park lab used four microwave stations. Xerox PARC, founded in 1970, hired many of his team; Apple later hired Xerox's. Engelbart's lab invented it all first.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: Leaves of Grass Published
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Brooklyn printer, essayist, and newspaper editor self-published a small quarto of 12 unrhymed, unmetered poems celebrating the American body politic in a language saturated with sexual frankness. It drew praise from Ralph Waldo Emerson and denunciation from almost everyone else. The author kept expanding and revising the volume for the rest of his life; the final 1892 "deathbed edition" contained over 400 poems.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1855 — Walt Whitman, self-published because no publisher would take it. He set much of it himself at a Brooklyn print shop. His job at the Department of the Interior was terminated in 1865 after the Secretary read a copy and called it obscene.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: Anne Frank's Diary Published
events.blurb: Two years after the liberation of Nazi concentration camps and the death of his teenage daughter in one of them, a Dutch businessman published, after several rejections, an edited version of the diary she had kept during the two years her family had spent hiding in a secret annex behind his Amsterdam office. The book was a modest Dutch bestseller; translated into over 70 languages, it became the most widely read personal account of the Holocaust.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1947 — Otto Frank published "Het Achterhuis" ("The Secret Annex"). Anne had died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen in February 1945, two months before liberation. The diary has sold over 30 million copies.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Jenner's First Vaccination
events.blurb: A 47-year-old English country doctor in Gloucestershire inoculated an 8-year-old boy with pus scraped from the hand of a milkmaid who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease related to smallpox but harmless in humans. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with actual smallpox. The boy did not get sick. The doctor wrote up his results, which transformed public health across the world over the next two centuries.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1796 — Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from vacca (Latin for cow). Jenner refused to patent the procedure despite the enormous potential fortune, insisting it was a gift to humanity. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only disease eliminated through vaccination.

events.title: Nightingale at Scutari
events.blurb: A 34-year-old British nurse arrived with 38 volunteer nurses at a filthy military hospital in a former Turkish barracks outside a Bosphorus capital, where British wounded from a Crimean war were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery at far higher rates than from combat wounds. Her reforms — sanitation, proper food, hand-washing, laundry — cut the death rate from 42 percent to 2 percent in six months. Her subsequent statistical advocacy reshaped nursing as a profession.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1854 — Florence Nightingale at Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul). Her nighttime rounds with an oil lamp produced the "Lady with the Lamp" sobriquet. She returned to London with chronic brucellosis, spent most of the rest of her life bedridden, and still wrote 200 books and reports. She lived to 90.

events.title: Aspirin Marketed
events.blurb: A German pharmaceutical and dye company began commercial sales of acetylsalicylic acid tablets under a trade name they had registered, marketed initially as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory. The active compound had been synthesized decades earlier, but this company had developed a stable, pure form suitable for mass production. The drug became one of the best-selling over-the-counter medications in history; low-dose versions are now used preventively against cardiovascular disease.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1899 — Bayer AG. Chief chemist Felix Hoffmann is traditionally credited; some historians credit Arthur Eichengrün, a Jewish colleague whose role was erased under Nazi-era Bayer PR. The drug's trade name came from a combination of "acetyl" and Spiraea, a plant source of salicylic acid.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First COVID-19 Vaccine Authorized
events.blurb: The US Food and Drug Administration issued an emergency use authorization for a novel mRNA-based vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, developed in less than a year from the publication of the virus's genetic sequence — a timescale previously thought impossible for a vaccine. The mRNA technology, which instructs the body's own cells to produce viral spike protein that the immune system then learns to recognize, had been in development for decades but had never been used in a licensed vaccine.
events.revealBlurb: December 11, 2020 — Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Moderna's similar mRNA vaccine followed December 18. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose basic mRNA research had been neglected for years, won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Over 13 billion COVID vaccine doses were administered globally in the first three years.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Marconi's Transatlantic Radio
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Italian-Irish electrical engineer and his assistants received, from a 300-metre wire antenna held aloft by a kite on a Newfoundland cliff, three short pulses — the letter S in Morse code — transmitted from a 25-kilowatt spark-gap generator in Cornwall, 3,400 kilometres away. The reception was brief, weak, and disputed by physicists who believed radio waves travelled only in straight lines and could not follow Earth's curvature. Subsequent experiments settled the argument.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 1901 — Guglielmo Marconi at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, receiving from Poldhu, Cornwall. He won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. The ionosphere's existence, which enables long-wave radio propagation around the planet, was not understood until the 1920s.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Magellan Sets Sail
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Portuguese-born captain, working for the Spanish crown because his own king had rejected his project, left a Sevillian port with five small ships and 270 men on a westward voyage to the spice-rich islands of Southeast Asia. He was convinced a sea passage through the Americas existed. He would find it — and a strait at the continent's southern tip is now named after him — but he would never see its other end.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1519 — Ferdinand Magellan. He was killed on the Philippine island of Mactan on April 27, 1521 by troops of the local chief Lapu-Lapu. One of his five ships completed the first circumnavigation — returning with 18 survivors and a load of cloves that covered the entire expedition's costs.

events.title: Council of Trent Opens
events.blurb: A general council of the Catholic Church, convened by the pope at a cathedral city in the Alpine foothills of northern Italy, opened with the task of responding to the Protestant Reformation. It met in three phases over 18 years, affirmed virtually every doctrine Protestants had rejected, standardized the Latin Mass, required bishops to reside in their dioceses, and launched the Counter-Reformation. Its decisions shaped Catholic practice for four centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 13, 1545 — opening of the Council of Trent. Its reforms hardened the Catholic/Protestant split rather than healing it. The Tridentine Latin Mass, established here, remained the standard form until the Second Vatican Council in 1965.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Awaara Released
events.blurb: A Raj Kapoor crime drama about a judge's illegitimate son — playing on the 1940s debate over heredity versus environment — became India's highest-grossing domestic release of the year and then, when dubbed and released abroad three years later, drew 64 million viewers in the Soviet Union alone, a record for any foreign film in that market. Its theme song became a street-singing anthem across Eurasia.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1951 — Raj Kapoor directed and starred. The song "Awaara Hoon" was so popular in the USSR, Turkey, and China that Soviet children grew up singing it phonetically in Hindi. Kapoor was reportedly stopped in Moscow streets for autographs.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: Pather Panchali Released
events.blurb: A first-time director shot a Bengali village drama across three years in fragments whenever he could afford to — including pawning his wife's jewellery to finish an opening sequence of a boy chasing a train through tall grass. It won a Humanist Prize at Cannes and launched a tradition of realist Indian cinema that bypassed Bombay entirely.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1955 — Satyajit Ray's debut. He was a commercial illustrator with no directing experience; the crew were mostly amateurs. The score was composed by an then-obscure sitarist named Ravi Shankar, recorded in a single 11-hour session. The West Bengal government funded its completion after seeing rough footage.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: The Fellowship of the Ring Released
events.blurb: A New Zealand director released the first of three films shot simultaneously in his homeland adapting a mid-20th-century English fantasy novel. The ensemble cast and landscape cinematography, the 5,000 days of digital effects by a Wellington-based studio, and the willingness to treat the fantasy material completely seriously pulled the genre from ghetto to respectability. The trilogy's final instalment would win 11 Oscars.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 2001 — Peter Jackson. The three films were shot over 438 days in New Zealand. Jackson's Weta Workshop became a world-leading effects house. The author's son Christopher Tolkien openly disliked the adaptations but inherited the royalty checks regardless.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Taft-Hartley Act Becomes Law
events.blurb: The Republican-controlled 80th Congress overrode President Harry Truman's veto, enacting the Labor-Management Relations Act — known as Taft-Hartley — which restricted union activities, banned secondary boycotts and solidarity strikes, permitted states to pass right-to-work laws, and required union officers to swear they were not Communists. The law fundamentally reshaped the relationship between organized labor and the federal government.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1947 — Washington, D.C. Truman called it a "slave labor bill" in his veto message, though he later used its provisions himself to break the 1952 steel strike. Union membership peaked at about 35% of the workforce in the late 1940s; by 2024 it had fallen to roughly 10%.

events.title: House Impeaches President Clinton
events.blurb: The House of Representatives voted to impeach President Bill Clinton on the 19th of that month, on charges of perjury before a grand jury (228–206) and obstruction of justice (221–212) arising from his false testimony about a sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton became only the second U.S. president ever to be impeached; the Senate acquitted him on both articles the following February.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1998 — U.S. Capitol. The vote occurred while U.S. warplanes were bombing Iraq (Operation Desert Fox), which the White House denied was timed to distract from the impeachment. House Speaker-designate Bob Livingston resigned that same day. Clinton's approval rating on the day of his impeachment was 73%.

events.title: January 6: U.S. Capitol Attacked
events.blurb: That morning, a mob of several thousand supporters of President Donald Trump stormed the U.S. Capitol building, breaching the chambers and offices of Congress as legislators were in the process of certifying the Electoral College results of the 2020 presidential election. The attack — the first violent breach of the Capitol since British forces burned it in 1814 — resulted in five deaths on the day and led to Trump's second impeachment.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 2021 — Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 people were charged with crimes related to the attack, the largest criminal investigation in U.S. Justice Department history. Congress completed the electoral certification at 3:44 am the following morning. The Capitol had not been occupied by hostile forces since August 24, 1814.

events.title: Apple's "1984" Super Bowl Ad
events.blurb: A 60-second commercial produced by a British director for a California computer company aired during the third quarter of the Super Bowl. The ad showed a dystopian audience of grey workers watching a Big-Brother-like speaker on a vast screen; an athletic woman in running clothes smashed the screen with a hammer. The product was the Macintosh computer. Apple's board had voted to kill the ad; the CEO insisted it air. It aired once.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1984 — directed by Ridley Scott. The ad ran nationally only that one time; it has since been shown as a promotion or film-clip thousands of times. Macintosh sales in its first 100 days exceeded expectations. The "1984" ad is still considered one of the greatest commercials ever made.

events.title: New Coke Launched
events.blurb: A 99-year-old American beverage company launched a reformulated version of its flagship cola, sweeter and smoother, aimed at winning back market share from Pepsi in a rivalry called the Cola Wars. Blind taste tests had shown a preference for the new recipe; actual consumer response, once they knew what they were drinking, was widespread rage. Letters of protest poured into Atlanta; soda fountains advertised the return of the original. 79 days later, the company announced the comeback of "Coca-Cola Classic."
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 1985 — Coca-Cola. The original formula returned as "Coca-Cola Classic" on July 11, 1985. New Coke eventually became "Coke II" in 1992 and was quietly discontinued in 2002. The whole episode is now a business-school case study in consumer-brand attachment.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
events.blurb: Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature premiered at a Los Angeles theatre — a project industry insiders had dismissed throughout its three-year production as "Disney's folly" that would bankrupt the studio. 800 artists had drawn 250,000 individual cel frames. The 83-minute film made nearly $8 million in its first release on a budget of $1.5 million, rescued the studio's finances, and launched the modern feature-animation industry.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1937 — Carthay Circle Theatre, Los Angeles. Disney received an honorary Oscar consisting of one regular-sized statuette and seven miniature ones, presented by Shirley Temple. Adjusted for inflation, the film is still among the top-grossing of all time.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Avatar Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director returning to live-action feature filmmaking after a 12-year absence released a 162-minute science-fiction epic set on a moon orbiting a distant gas giant, shot with a new custom-built 3D camera system and populated by performance-captured 3-metre-tall blue aliens. The film's production had taken four years after the technology he needed had taken another decade. It became the highest-grossing film of all time and held the title for ten years.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2009 — James Cameron. The film grossed $2.9 billion on its initial run, briefly lost the title to Avengers: Endgame, then retook it with a 2021 re-release in China. Cameron had first written the treatment in 1994.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.

events.title: Radium Announced
events.blurb: A husband-and-wife chemistry team announced the isolation of a new radioactive element extracted from several tonnes of pitchblende ore, reporting it was approximately 900 times more radioactive than uranium. The woman researcher would go on to become the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different scientific disciplines.

events.title: Radium Discovered
events.blurb: After months of processing tonnes of uranium ore residue in a leaky shed, two researchers announced the existence of a second highly radioactive element — far more active per gram than uranium alone. The new element glowed faintly in the dark, making the laboratory notebooks radioactive enough to be hazardous even today. The work established radioactivity as an atomic property rather than a chemical reaction.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 1898 — Marie and Pierre Curie's notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection; researchers must sign a waiver to view them in the French national library. Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Photoelectric Effect Explained
events.blurb: A paper explained why shining light on a metal surface ejects electrons only when the light exceeds a threshold frequency — never for very bright low-frequency light — by proposing that light itself travels in discrete energy packets rather than continuous waves. The finding resolved a long-standing paradox and extended the quantum idea from heat radiation to light, fundamentally changing the understanding of what light is.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1905 — this was the paper that explicitly won Einstein the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not relativity. When the Nobel Committee finally awarded it (sixteen years late), they cited this discovery specifically. Einstein reportedly joked that the committee must have found relativity too controversial.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Leif Erikson Reaches Vinland
events.blurb: A Norse explorer sailing west from a Greenland settlement founded by his father made landfall on a wooded North American coast, probably in what is now Newfoundland. His expedition built a small settlement and wintered there before returning. It was the first documented European presence in the Americas, and it would be almost entirely forgotten for five centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1000 CE — Leif, son of Erik the Red. The site at L'Anse aux Meadows was confirmed archaeologically only in 1960. Later expeditions established small colonies that died out, apparently after conflict with local Indigenous people the Norse called "Skrælings."

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.blurb: A 44-year-old tribal chieftain named Temüjin, having spent two decades defeating his rivals across the eastern steppe, was acclaimed "Universal Ruler" at an assembly of chieftains beside a sacred river. Within two decades his cavalry armies would sack Beijing, overrun Persia, and reach the Adriatic, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 — at the Onon River. The title "Genghis Khan" is a western rendering; contemporary Mongol sources call him Činggis Qa'an. Genetic studies suggest roughly 16 million men alive today descend from his Y-chromosome line.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: Grand Tour Launch
events.blurb: A Titan IIIE rocket launched a 722-kilogram probe carrying a gold-plated phonograph record with greetings in 55 languages and 116 images. Its trajectory used gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn to reach escape velocity.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: Chauvet Cave Paintings
events.blurb: Deep inside a limestone gorge in southern France, artists of the Upper Paleolithic ventured hundreds of metres into darkness with torches of burning pine and painted more than 400 animals onto the walls — rhinos, horses, cave lions, mammoths — using charcoal and red ochre. The images show sophisticated techniques: perspective, shading, motion. They would remain sealed behind a rockslide until rediscovered by three cavers in 1994.
events.revealBlurb: c. 30,000 BCE — Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche. Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal remains controversial; estimates span 32,000-30,000 BCE. A meticulous replica opened to tourists in 2015; the original site is restricted to scientists to preserve a fragile microclimate.

events.title: Leonardo da Vinci Dies
events.blurb: A 67-year-old Florentine polymath died in a small château in the Loire Valley, where the French king had invited him to retire. On the easel beside his bed was an unfinished portrait of a Florentine merchant's wife that he had carried with him for sixteen years and never delivered to the man who had commissioned it. The king would acquire the painting from his executor; the subject's name, Lisa Gherardini, would eventually become the most famous name in art.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 1519 — Leonardo at Clos Lucé, Amboise. The portrait is the Mona Lisa, now in the Louvre, which he had begun around 1503. He bequeathed his notebooks, which he wrote in mirror script, to his assistant Francesco Melzi.

events.title: Van Gogh Cuts Off His Ear
events.blurb: After a violent argument with a fellow painter who had been living with him at a small yellow house in Provence for nine weeks, a 35-year-old Dutch artist cut off part of his own left ear with a razor, wrapped it in newspaper, and walked through the rain to deliver the package to a woman at a nearby brothel.
