He spent the night lying in a pool of blood. The fellow painter left the next morning. The injured man was committed to an asylum.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1888 — Vincent van Gogh; the houseguest was Paul Gauguin. He painted "Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear" within weeks. He sold only one painting in his lifetime and shot himself 19 months later in a Paris suburb.

events.title: Munch's The Scream
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Norwegian painter completed the first version of a composition he had been sketching for years, showing a androgynous figure with an egg-shaped face and open mouth on a bridge above a blood-orange sky. The painter later wrote of the walk at dusk during which he had felt "a shriek passing through nature." He produced four versions across several decades; two have been stolen, and both were recovered.
events.revealBlurb: 1893 — Edvard Munch. The sky's colour may be real: it has been linked to the atmospheric effects of the Krakatoa eruption ten years earlier. The Oslo theft in 1994 happened during the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics. The thieves left a note: "Thanks for the poor security."

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Indian National Congress Founded
events.blurb: Seventy-two delegates — mostly English-educated Indian lawyers, journalists, and teachers, along with a few sympathetic Britons — met at a college in a western Indian port city for a three-day conference to petition the colonial government for greater Indian representation in its administration. The polite gathering would, over six decades, become the vehicle of a mass independence movement.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1885 — Bombay (now Mumbai). The prime mover was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, who believed organized political expression would prevent revolution. He was half right.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
events.blurb: Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on the Bengali-speaking eastern wing of its own country, displacing an estimated 10 million refugees across the border into India. India intervened militarily; within thirteen days it had driven the Pakistani army to capitulate in a Bengali capital, where 93,000 surrendered in the largest military surrender since WWII. A new nation was born.
events.revealBlurb: December 3-16, 1971 — victory at the Instrument of Surrender at Ramna Race Course, Dhaka. Bangladesh Liberation Day is December 16. Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw commanded the Indian effort; Lt. General A.A.K. Niazi signed the surrender.

events.title: Right to Information Act
events.blurb: A law guaranteeing any citizen of the country the right to request information from public authorities — and compelling officials to respond within 30 days or face personal penalties — came into force after a decade-long campaign driven by rural social movements in a western state. It quickly became one of the most-used such laws in the world, exposing corruption from village panchayats to the prime minister's office.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 2005 — RTI Act. Aruna Roy's Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan was the movement's backbone. Its origins lay in drought-era sit-ins demanding to see the village wage registers. More than a hundred RTI activists have been murdered since passage.

events.title: Truman Doctrine
events.blurb: Addressing a joint session of Congress, a U.S. president requested $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey and announced a sweeping new foreign policy: the United States would support "free peoples" resisting armed minorities or outside pressures. The speech committed America to global containment of communism.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1947 — Harry Truman needed just 18 minutes. Behind the rhetoric: Britain, bankrupted by war, had quietly told Washington it could no longer prop up the Greek government. America stepped into the imperial vacuum.

events.title: Gulf of Tonkin Incident
events.blurb: A U.S. Navy destroyer reported it had been attacked by small torpedo boats off the North Vietnamese coast. Two nights later, the same destroyer and a second reported a second attack in bad weather — an attack that likely never happened. Within days, Congress passed a resolution authorizing the president to use "all necessary measures" in Southeast Asia, opening the door to full-scale war.
events.revealBlurb: August 2 and 4, 1964 — the second "attack" was almost certainly radar ghosts and jumpy sonar operators. The resolution passed the House 416-0 and the Senate 88-2. Declassified NSA documents in 2005 confirmed the fabrication.

events.title: Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan
events.blurb: Thousands of Soviet paratroopers and mechanized divisions crossed into a central Asian country to prop up a failing Marxist government, assassinating the sitting president in the process and installing a more pliable replacement. The operation was supposed to last weeks. Instead it dragged on for nearly a decade, bleeding the Soviet treasury, radicalizing a generation of fighters, and helping bring the superpower down.
events.revealBlurb: December 24-27, 1979 — the intervention cost the USSR an estimated 15,000 dead and 35,000 wounded. The US, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan funneled billions in arms to the mujahideen, some of whom would later form al-Qaeda.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.blurb: An East German spokesman, reading hastily from a note and misunderstanding its contents, announced at a televised press conference that new travel rules would take effect "immediately." Within hours, tens of thousands of jubilant East Berliners massed at the crossings. Confused border guards, receiving no clear orders, simply let them through. People scrambled onto the concrete barrier with hammers.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 1989 — the spokesman was Günter Schabowski, who had skimmed the briefing note just before the press conference. Asked when the rules took effect, he shrugged: "As far as I know — immediately." The wall, built in a single night 28 years earlier, came down in a single night too.

events.title: Romanian Revolution
events.blurb: Within ten days, a dictator who had ruled a Balkan nation for 24 years lost control of a mass demonstration, fled the capital by helicopter, was captured, given a two-hour military tribunal, and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day alongside his wife. It was the only violent collapse among the eastern bloc regimes that fell at the time.
events.revealBlurb: December 16-25, 1989 — Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu. Soldiers actually had to be ordered to stop shooting them — they kept firing at the already-dead bodies. Ceaușescu's final request was to sing the Internationale. It was denied.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: William the Conqueror Crowned
events.blurb: Ten weeks after winning a decisive battle on the south coast of England, the Norman duke who had invaded was crowned king at a Westminster abbey. During the coronation, Norman guards outside the abbey mistook acclamations for riot and set fire to nearby houses; the new king was hurriedly anointed while smoke drifted through the doors. He would never be popular with his new subjects.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1066 — Westminster Abbey. William spent the next two decades building castles, compiling the Domesday Book, and crushing rebellions. He was buried in Caen, and his tomb was opened, profaned, and emptied of bones during the French Revolution.

events.title: Murder of Thomas Becket
events.blurb: Four knights, prompted by an angry outburst from their king over the head of the English church, rode to a cathedral in southern England and hacked the archbishop to death in his own nave after he refused to reconsider his excommunications of clergy who had sided with the king. The murder scandalized Christendom; pilgrimages to the martyr's tomb began within weeks and continued for 368 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 29, 1170 — Canterbury Cathedral, Thomas Becket killed by four knights of Henry II. The king's supposed outburst — "Who will rid me of this turbulent priest?" — may be apocryphal. Becket was canonized within three years; T.S. Eliot turned the story into "Murder in the Cathedral."

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Fall of Granada
events.blurb: The last Muslim ruler of an Andalusian emirate, besieged for seven months in his Alhambra palace, handed over its keys to Castilian and Aragonese monarchs and rode into exile, reportedly sighing at his final view from a mountain pass. The surrender ended 781 years of Muslim political presence on the Iberian peninsula. The same monarchs, three months later, would commission an Italian sailor to seek a western route to Asia.
events.revealBlurb: January 2, 1492 — Ferdinand and Isabella accept the surrender of Muhammad XII (Boabdil). His mother is said to have told him: "You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man." Columbus was at the Alhambra that summer presenting his proposal.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Black Summer Bushfires
events.blurb: A prolonged drought and record heat fueled a six-month season of bushfires that burned 24 million hectares of southeastern Australia — an area larger than England. 33 people died directly; several hundred more from smoke. An estimated one billion wild animals perished. Smoke drifted across the Pacific and circled the globe.
events.revealBlurb: September 2019 – March 2020 — Australia. Images of koalas drinking from cyclists' water bottles and a town sheltering under blood-red skies went viral. Firefighters came from 12 countries. The season ended just as COVID-19 lockdowns began, compounding public trauma.

events.title: First ARPANET Message
events.blurb: A graduate student at a California university tried to log in remotely to a computer at a research institute 560 kilometres north. He typed "L," then "O," then tried to type "G" — and the receiving computer crashed. The first ever message transmitted between two computers on what would grow into the global network was thus the two-letter sequence "lo."
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1969 — UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute. The student was Charley Kline. ARPANET was funded by the Pentagon to enable communication after a nuclear strike. The network went from 4 nodes to 37 in three years.

events.title: Y2K Rollover
events.blurb: As the world's time zones successively crossed the boundary between the 20th and 21st centuries, decades of doomsday predictions — that computer systems storing years as two digits would interpret "00" as 1900 and crash vital infrastructure — largely failed to materialize. An estimated $300 billion had been spent worldwide on remediation code. Whether the peaceful transition vindicated the expense or exposed it as overblown remains contested.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 2000 — New Zealand and Pacific islands hit midnight first, without incident. Actual bugs did occur — a French meteorological satellite briefly misreported dates, some slot machines froze, a few nuclear plants had cooling-monitor glitches — but nothing catastrophic. The fix, written in COBOL in the 1990s, may be the largest software project ever.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: Gangnam Style Hits 1 Billion Views
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper satirizing the upper-class culture of a Seoul neighborhood crossed a threshold no online video had previously reached, having accumulated a billion views on a major video platform in just over five months. Its horse-riding dance became a global meme and introduced a generation of Western audiences to K-pop. It broke the video platform's 32-bit view counter, forcing an engineering upgrade.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2012 — PSY's "Gangnam Style." It held the title of most-viewed YouTube video for five years before being overtaken by "Despacito." The counter overflow bug was quietly patched in 2014 when the video hit over 2 billion views.

events.title: Colosseum Inaugurated
events.blurb: A Roman emperor inaugurated a 50,000-capacity elliptical amphitheatre in the capital with 100 consecutive days of gladiatorial games, executions, and staged hunts that killed 9,000 animals. The structure was four stories tall, constructed in travertine and concrete, with a retractable canvas awning (velarium) to shade the spectators. Its name comes from the colossal statue of an earlier emperor that stood nearby. Three quarters of the building still stands today.
events.revealBlurb: 80 CE — inaugurated by Emperor Titus, son of Vespasian who had started construction eight years earlier. The colossal statue in question was of Nero, which Vespasian had rededicated as the sun god. Most of the travertine facing was stripped in medieval times for Renaissance building projects.

events.title: Dome of the Rock Completed
events.blurb: An Umayyad caliph completed an octagonal Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount of a holy city, sheltering a rock Muslims believe the prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven from. Its distinctive gilded dome, 20 metres across, shimmered over the Old City; its interior walls were covered in Byzantine-style mosaics in golden, green, and blue. It is the oldest extant Islamic building and one of the earliest examples of monumental Islamic architecture.
events.revealBlurb: 691 CE — Caliph Abd al-Malik in Jerusalem. Built on the Noble Sanctuary, also the site of the ancient Jewish Second Temple. The gilded dome has been re-gilded many times; the current covering, added in 1993, used 80 kilograms of gold donated by King Hussein of Jordan.

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: Burj Khalifa Opens
events.blurb: A 828-metre tapering skyscraper — Y-shaped in plan, with a buttressed central core — opened in a Gulf financial center as the tallest building in the world, dramatically taller than the previous record holder. Its construction had begun at the height of a regional real-estate bubble; by opening it had lost over 60 percent of its value and been taken over by a neighbouring emirate, after whose ruler the tower was hastily renamed. Its name had been "Burj Dubai" during construction.
events.revealBlurb: January 4, 2010 — architect Adrian Smith at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The renamed "Burj Khalifa" honored Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, whose government bailed out Dubai during the financial crisis. Tom Cruise dangled from the outside in "Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol" (2011).

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Storming of the Bastille
events.blurb: A mob of several thousand Parisians, enraged by the dismissal of a popular finance minister and rumours of royal military preparations, stormed a royal fortress prison on the city's eastern edge in search of gunpowder stored there. The garrison surrendered after a bloody four-hour assault; the commandant was murdered and his head carried on a pike through the streets. The prison itself held only seven prisoners. The date became the French national holiday.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1789 — the Bastille. Seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics, one aristocrat imprisoned by his family. Marquis de Launay, the commandant, is the famous head on the pike. Parisians began demolishing the fortress the next morning; it was fully down within three months.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Haiti Declares Independence
events.blurb: A former slave turned general, addressing a small crowd at a town on a Caribbean island, declared the independence of a new sovereign state that replaced a French sugar colony. It took the name of the original Taíno indigenous word for the island. It was the first independent state in Latin America, the only one to emerge from a successful slave revolt, and the second republic in the Western hemisphere. European powers reacted with diplomatic ostracism; the United States refused recognition for 58 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1804 — Jean-Jacques Dessalines at Gonaïves, Haiti. France demanded reparations for "lost property" — 150 million francs — that Haiti finished paying only in 1947. The combination of debt, ostracism, and internal strife has shaped Haitian poverty for two centuries.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Ben Johnson Stripped of Gold
events.blurb: A Canadian sprinter who had won the 100-metre final at a Seoul Summer Olympics three days earlier in a world-record 9.79 seconds was stripped of his gold medal after testing positive for the anabolic steroid stanozolol. His urine sample, taken minutes after the race, showed levels consistent with recent deliberate use. The silver medallist — an American who had won the 1987 world title — was elevated to gold. He too would later be caught doping.
events.revealBlurb: September 27, 1988 — Ben Johnson stripped of gold; Carl Lewis elevated. Of the eight finalists, six were later connected to performance-enhancing drug use. Johnson was eventually banned for life after a second positive in 1993. The Dubin Inquiry that followed his case reshaped anti-doping policy.

events.title: Michael Jordan's First Retirement
events.blurb: Three months after winning his third straight NBA championship and four months after his father had been murdered in a highway robbery, the 30-year-old best basketball player in the world held a press conference announcing his retirement from the game. He had "lost the desire to play," he said. Months later he was playing minor-league baseball for a Chicago White Sox affiliate. He would return to the NBA 17 months after his retirement, winning three more championships.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1993 — Michael Jordan. His AA baseball season with the Birmingham Barons ended with a .202 batting average. His return to the NBA, announced March 18, 1995 with the two-word press release "I'm back," drew him to four more championships (1996, 1997, 1998) before a second retirement, then a third comeback with the Washington Wizards.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott Ends
events.blurb: After 381 days of Black residents walking, carpooling, and riding Black-owned taxis rather than boarding segregated city buses, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower-court ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The next morning, Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks boarded an integrated bus in the front seats. The boycott had nearly bankrupted the transit system.
events.revealBlurb: December 20, 1956 — Martin Luther King rose to national prominence via the boycott. The organizing bureau ran car-pool lots that transported 30,000 people a day. Many Black women walked miles to work for over a year. "My feet is tired," one said famously, "but my soul is rested."

events.title: SNCC Founded
events.blurb: At a North Carolina conference convened by a veteran activist, 200 student sit-in leaders from across the South formed a new grassroots organization to coordinate direct-action campaigns independently of older civil rights groups. The students were younger, more confrontational, and willing to risk their lives; many became the foot soldiers of the Freedom Rides, Freedom Summer, and Selma.
events.revealBlurb: April 17, 1960 — Raleigh, NC. Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, commonly pronounced "snick." Organizer Ella Baker convinced the students to stay independent rather than fold into Martin Luther King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Stokely Carmichael led it during the "Black Power" turn in 1966.

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.
